:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $f'(x) - 3\sin(2x) = 0.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
f'(x) = 3\sin{2x}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the General Solution of a Differential Equation Using Integration

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} = x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Integrating the equation once, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating a second time, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C)\,\text{d}x \\ y & =\frac{1}{6}{x}^{3}+Cx+D\end{aligned}
$$

Note that because we had a second-order equation, our general solution contains *two* arbitrary constants, $C$ and $D.$ We cannot combine them, because $C$ is being multiplied by $x$ while $D$ is not.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the particular solution to the differential equation below that satisfies the condition $f(0)=2.$

$$
f'(x) - \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} = 0
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation to give

$$
f'(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2}.
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x,$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ f(x) & =3\int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So our general solution is $f(x) = 3\arctan{x} + C.$ To find a particular solution, we substitute the condition $f(0) = 2$ into our solution and obtain a value for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ 2 & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)+C \\ 2 & =0+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is 

$$
f(x)=3\arctan x + 2.
$$
